title: The Debt I Paid Without Leaving My Name
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Last month, I was standing in line at the small pharmacy near my office when I overheard a woman apologizing to the cashier.
Narrator: [reflective] She was short on money for her son's medicine, and she kept asking if she could pay the rest tomorrow, although the cashier looked unsure.
Narrator: [gently] I didn't know her, and she never noticed me standing behind her, because she was too embarrassed to look up at anyone.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I could have simply paid the difference right there and told her it was from me, and she would have thanked me immediately.
Narrator: [determined] Instead, I asked the cashier quietly to add the missing amount to my own bill, and to please not mention who paid it.
Narrator: [honestly] The cashier looked confused, so I explained that if the woman knew, she might feel like she owed me something, and I didn't want that.
Narrator: [reflective] I walked out before she finished her purchase, so I never even saw her face clearly, and I still don't know her name.
Narrator: [with feeling] For a few days afterward, I kept wanting to tell my wife what happened, mostly because I felt proud of myself.
Narrator: [honestly] Then I realized that wanting to tell the story was exactly the danger my father warned me about years ago.
Narrator: [thoughtful] He always said that a good deed shared too quickly often loses its sincerity, because part of us starts performing for an audience.
Narrator: [gently] So I stayed quiet, although it was harder than I expected, because silence sometimes feels heavier than speaking.
Narrator: [peacefully] Now, whenever I pass that pharmacy, I think of her for a moment, hope her son is healthy, and then I simply keep walking.
Narrator: [sincere] I have learned that some good deeds are meant to stay between you, the moment, and Allah, without ever becoming a story you tell later.

quiz.question: Where was the narrator standing when he overheard the woman?
options: In line at a small pharmacy
quiz.explanation: He was standing in line at the small pharmacy near his office when he overheard her.

quiz.question: What was the woman apologizing about?
options: Being short on money for her son's medicine
quiz.explanation: She was short on money for her son's medicine and asked to pay the rest later.

quiz.question: What did the narrator ask the cashier to do?
options: Add the missing amount to his own bill without saying who paid
quiz.explanation: He asked the cashier to quietly add the missing amount to his bill and not mention who paid.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's father once warn him about?
options: A good deed shared too quickly often loses its sincerity
quiz.explanation: His father warned him that a good deed shared too quickly often loses its sincerity.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator stay quiet about what he did?
options: He didn't want the deed to become a story he tells
His wife told him not to speak
quiz.explanation: He learned that some good deeds are meant to stay between him, the moment, and Allah.

title: Two Brothers Decide Who Will Move In With Father
script: Yusuf: [tired] Fikri, we need to actually decide this today. Father can't keep living alone since his fall last month.
Fikri: [thoughtful] I know, although I keep hoping a solution will appear without either of us needing to change our whole life.
Yusuf: [gently] There isn't a solution like that, honestly. One of us has to move closer, or he has to move in with one of us.
Fikri: [hesitant] My apartment is small, and my job requires long hours, so I'm not sure I could care for him properly right now.
Yusuf: [understanding] I'm not blaming you. I'm just trying to be realistic about what each of us can actually offer him.
Fikri: [quietly] Can I be honest? Part of me feels guilty even discussing this like a schedule, instead of something we should just want to do.
Yusuf: [warmly] I feel that too, but planning carefully doesn't mean we love him less. It means we want to take care of him properly.
Fikri: [reflective] You're right. So what are you proposing, exactly?
Yusuf: [thoughtful] I have an extra room, and although my schedule is busy too, I can rearrange some mornings around his needs.
Fikri: [relieved] Are you sure? I don't want you carrying this alone while I visit occasionally and feel like a good son from a distance.
Yusuf: [gently] I'm sure, but I need you to visit often, not out of guilt, but because he genuinely lights up whenever you walk in.
Fikri: [sincere] I promise I will, every weekend if I can manage it, and I'll help with his medical bills completely.
Yusuf: [warmly] That sounds fair. This isn't about who does more. It's about making sure he never feels forgotten by either of us.
Fikri: [with feeling] He used to carry both of us on his shoulders when we were small. This feels like a small way to return that.
Yusuf: [peacefully] Exactly. Let's tell him together tonight, so he knows this decision came from both of us equally.
Fikri: [determined] Agreed. And Yusuf, thank you for offering the room before I even had to ask you properly.

quiz.question: Why can't the father keep living alone?
quiz.explanation: Yusuf says their father can't keep living alone since his fall last month.

quiz.question: Why is Fikri unsure he can care for his father right now?
options: His apartment is small and his job requires long hours
He is moving to another country
quiz.explanation: Fikri says his apartment is small and his job requires long hours.

quiz.question: What does Yusuf offer to do?
options: Let their father move into his extra room
Ask their father to live alone
quiz.explanation: Yusuf offers his extra room and says he can rearrange some mornings around their father's needs.

quiz.question: What does Fikri promise to do instead?
options: Visit often and help with medical bills
quiz.explanation: Fikri promises to visit every weekend if he can and help with medical bills completely.

quiz.question: What do the brothers decide to do that night?
options: Argue in front of their father
Tell their father the decision together
Ask their father to choose alone
quiz.explanation: Yusuf suggests telling their father together that night, so he knows the decision came from both of them.

title: The Wallet I Found on the Train Platform
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] Yesterday evening, I found a leather wallet lying near the train platform, and it looked like it had fallen out of someone's bag in a hurry.
Narrator: [honestly] Inside, there was a large amount of cash, several bank cards, and an identification card with a photo and an address.
Narrator: [reflective] My first thought, embarrassingly, was how much that cash could actually help me this month, since rent was already overdue.
Narrator: [with feeling] I stood there for almost a minute, holding it, feeling a strange, uncomfortable pull between two very different decisions.
Narrator: [determined] Then I thought about how frightened I would feel if I lost something that important, and how badly I would want a stranger to be honest.
Narrator: [gently] So I checked the address on the identification card, and because it wasn't too far, I decided to walk there directly instead of calling first.
Narrator: [nervously] An older man opened the door, and when he saw the wallet in my hand, his whole face changed from worry to disbelief.
Narrator: [warmly] He kept saying thank you again and again, and he tried to give me some of the cash as a reward for returning it.
Narrator: [sincere] I refused politely, and I told him that returning it wasn't something I wanted to be paid for, because that would change what it actually meant.
Narrator: [reflective] He asked why I would walk so far out of my way for a stranger, especially while clearly struggling financially myself.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I told him honestly that I wanted to be able to pray that night without a heavy, guilty feeling sitting quietly in my chest.
Narrator: [peacefully] Walking home afterward, my rent was still overdue, and nothing about my situation had changed, yet I felt lighter than I had in weeks.
Narrator: [warmly] Honesty didn't solve my problem that night, but it reminded me exactly who I still want to be, even when nobody would have known otherwise.

quiz.question: Where did the narrator find the wallet?
quiz.explanation: She found a leather wallet lying near the train platform.

quiz.question: What was the narrator's first thought upon finding the cash?
options: How much the cash could help her since rent was overdue
To count the money for fun
quiz.explanation: Her first thought, embarrassingly, was how much the cash could help her since rent was already overdue.

quiz.question: How did the narrator decide to return the wallet?
options: She checked the address and walked there directly
She left it with the police
quiz.explanation: She checked the address on the identification card and walked there directly instead of calling first.

quiz.question: How did the man react when he saw the wallet?
options: His face changed from worry to disbelief, and he thanked her repeatedly
He accused her of stealing it
quiz.explanation: His whole face changed from worry to disbelief, and he kept thanking her again and again.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator refuse the reward money?
options: She thought it was too little
Being paid would change what the honest act actually meant
She was afraid of the man
quiz.explanation: She refused because being paid for returning it would change what the act actually meant to her.

title: A Study Group Faces a Temptation to Cheat
script: Doni: [excited] Wulan, look what I found. Someone posted photos of tomorrow's exam questions in our class group chat.
Wulan: [surprised] Wait, seriously? Where did those even come from?
Doni: [casual] Apparently someone in the earlier class session photographed the paper and shared it before anyone noticed.
Wulan: [uneasy] Doni, I'm not sure we should even be looking at this, honestly.
Doni: [defensive] Everyone in the group chat has already seen it. We would just be at a disadvantage if we didn't look too.
Wulan: [thoughtful] That logic feels backward to me. Because others did something wrong doesn't mean it becomes okay for us.
Doni: [frustrated] This exam decides half our final grade, Wulan. You know how much I've struggled with this subject all semester.
Wulan: [gently] I know you've struggled, and I've watched you study late almost every night. That effort deserves an honest result, not a stolen one.
Doni: [quietly] But what if I fail anyway, even after using these? At least this way I'd have a real chance.
Wulan: [sincere] Would it really feel like your success though, if you knew the truth about how you got there?
Doni: [silent for a moment] No, honestly, it probably wouldn't. I think I already knew that before I even showed you the photos.
Wulan: [warmly] Let's study together tonight instead, properly, using our actual notes, and whatever grade we get will at least belong to us.
Doni: [reflective] Part of me is still scared it won't be enough, though.
Wulan: [gently] Maybe it won't be, and that's frightening, but I'd rather fail honestly than pass while feeling like a fraud every time I remember it.
Doni: [determined] Okay. Delete the photos from your phone too. I don't want the temptation sitting there tomorrow morning before the exam.
Wulan: [smiling] Already deleting mine. Now, pass me your notes on chapter six, because I still don't understand half of it.
Doni: [with a small laugh] Deal. Let's earn this one the hard way, together.

quiz.question: What did Doni find in the class group chat?
quiz.explanation: Doni found photos of tomorrow's exam questions posted in the class group chat.

quiz.question: What is Doni's first argument for looking at the photos?
options: Everyone else has already seen it, so they would be at a disadvantage otherwise
quiz.explanation: Doni argues that everyone has already seen it, so they would be at a disadvantage if they didn't look too.

quiz.question: How does Wulan respond to that argument?
options: She says others doing something wrong doesn't make it okay for them
She says the exam doesn't matter
She reports Doni to the teacher
quiz.explanation: Wulan says that logic feels backward, because others doing something wrong doesn't make it okay for them too.

quiz.question: What does Doni admit when Wulan asks if it would feel like real success?
options: No, it probably wouldn't feel like his own success
He would tell everyone about it
quiz.explanation: Doni admits it probably wouldn't feel like real success, and that he already suspected that before showing Wulan.

quiz.question: What do Wulan and Doni decide to do at the end?
options: Delete the photos and study together honestly
quiz.explanation: They agree to delete the photos and study together using their actual notes instead.

title: The Overpaid Fare and the Long Drive Back
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] I have been driving a taxi for eleven years now, and most nights blend together into one long, tired blur.
Narrator: [reflective] But one night last spring still stands out clearly, because of something small that happened right at the very end of a ride.
Narrator: [honestly] A young tourist got into my car late at night, exhausted after a long flight, and asked me to take him to his hotel.
Narrator: [gently] He didn't speak our language well, and he seemed nervous about handling unfamiliar money, so he simply handed me a folded bundle of cash.
Narrator: [thoughtful] He said, please just take what I owe you, since I don't fully understand the currency yet after arriving today.
Narrator: [with feeling] I counted it later under a streetlight and realized he had accidentally given me almost four times the actual fare.
Narrator: [reflective] It was already close to midnight, my shift had technically ended, and I was genuinely exhausted after a long, difficult day of driving.
Narrator: [determined] Still, I turned my taxi around and drove back toward his hotel, because keeping that money felt like stealing from someone who trusted me completely.
Narrator: [honestly] When I found him in the lobby, he looked confused, and then embarrassed, once I explained his simple counting mistake.
Narrator: [warmly] He tried to insist I keep the extra money anyway, calling it a generous tip for driving all the way back so late.
Narrator: [sincere] I told him gently that returning it wasn't generosity on my part, it was simply what honesty required of me that night.
Narrator: [peacefully] He shook my hand for a long moment before finally going upstairs, and I drove home feeling something warmer than any large tip could have given me.
Narrator: [warmly] My family still doesn't fully understand why I turned down that extra money during such a tiring week, but I've never once regretted the decision.

quiz.question: How long has the narrator been driving a taxi?
quiz.explanation: He says he has been driving a taxi for eleven years.

quiz.question: Why did the tourist hand him a folded bundle of cash?
options: He wanted to give a huge tip
He didn't fully understand the currency yet
quiz.explanation: The tourist said he didn't fully understand the currency yet, so he asked the driver to take what he owed.

quiz.question: What did the narrator discover when he counted the money later?
options: It was almost four times the actual fare
It was less than the fare
quiz.explanation: He realized the tourist had accidentally given him almost four times the actual fare.

quiz.question: What did the narrator do after discovering the mistake?
options: He turned his taxi around and drove back to the hotel
quiz.explanation: Even though his shift had ended and he was exhausted, he turned his taxi around and drove back.

quiz.question: How did the narrator describe his reason for returning the money?
options: It was generosity on his part
It was simply what honesty required of him
He was afraid of getting caught
quiz.explanation: He told the tourist that returning it wasn't generosity, it was simply what honesty required of him that night.

title: A Call-In Show About the Boy Who Cleans the Mosque
script: Radio Host: [warmly] Good evening, listeners. Tonight, Ibu Sari is calling in with a story about her fifteen-year-old son. Welcome to the show.
Caller: [pleasantly] Thank you for having me. I almost didn't call, because my son would be embarrassed if he knew I was telling this.
Radio Host: [curious] Then let's protect his privacy a little. Can you tell us what he's been doing?
Caller: [warmly] For almost a year now, he wakes up at dawn every Friday and walks to our neighborhood mosque before anyone else arrives.
Radio Host: [interested] What does he do once he gets there so early?
Caller: [thoughtful] He sweeps the floors, arranges the prayer mats neatly, and cleans the bathrooms, completely on his own, without anyone asking him to.
Radio Host: [surprised] That's unusual for someone his age. How did you first discover this habit?
Caller: [reflective] Honestly, I found out by accident when the mosque caretaker mentioned it to my husband, thinking we already knew about it.
Radio Host: [curious] Had your son never mentioned it himself?
Caller: [gently] Never once, not to us, not to his friends, not even to his older sister, who he tells almost everything else.
Radio Host: [thoughtful] Did you ask him why he keeps it so private?
Caller: [honestly] I did, carefully, one evening, and he simply said he didn't want people thanking him, because that wasn't the point of doing it.
Radio Host: [touched] What did he say the actual point was?
Caller: [warmly] He said he wanted at least one thing in his week that belonged only to him and Allah, without anyone else's opinion involved.
Radio Host: [thoughtful] That's a mature thought for someone so young.
Caller: [proudly] It surprised me too. I used to worry he was too quiet, too serious for his age, but now I understand it differently.
Radio Host: [warmly] Thank you for sharing this, Ibu Sari. I imagine many parents listening tonight needed to hear a story like this.
Caller: [sincerely] Thank you. I only called because I think quiet goodness deserves to be noticed sometimes, even from far away, even without his name.

quiz.question: What does the caller's son do every Friday at dawn?
options: He walks to the mosque and cleans it before anyone arrives
quiz.explanation: He wakes up at dawn every Friday and walks to the mosque before anyone else arrives to clean it.

quiz.question: How long has the son been doing this?
quiz.explanation: The caller says he has been doing this for almost a year now.

quiz.question: How did the mother first find out about it?
options: The mosque caretaker mentioned it to her husband by accident
quiz.explanation: She found out by accident when the mosque caretaker mentioned it to her husband, assuming they already knew.

quiz.question: Why did the son say he keeps it private?
options: He didn't want people thanking him, since that wasn't the point
His parents told him to hide it
He thought it was against the rules
quiz.explanation: He said he didn't want people thanking him, because that wasn't the point of doing it.

quiz.question: What did the son say he wanted from this habit?
options: One thing in his week that belonged only to him and Allah
To become well known at the mosque
quiz.explanation: He said he wanted at least one thing in his week that belonged only to him and Allah, without anyone else's opinion.

title: What My Grandmother Never Overcharged For
script: Narrator: [warmly] My grandmother sold fabric at the market for over thirty years, and everyone in our town knew her simply as Mbah Fabric.
Narrator: [reflective] She wasn't the cheapest seller there, but customers still walked past three other stalls just to buy from her specifically.
Narrator: [thoughtful] As a teenager, I once asked her why people were so loyal, since her prices weren't actually the lowest around.
Narrator: [gently] She said, because they know I will never lie about the quality, even when a lie would earn me more money that day.
Narrator: [honestly] I remember watching her once refuse to sell a torn piece of fabric to a customer who hadn't even noticed the small tear herself.
Narrator: [curious] I asked her afterward why she pointed it out, since the customer clearly would have bought it anyway without complaint.
Narrator: [warmly] She said that silence, in that moment, would have been the same as lying, even though technically she said nothing false at all.
Narrator: [thoughtful] That idea confused me for years, because I always thought honesty only meant avoiding actual false statements, nothing more complicated than that.
Narrator: [reflective] Later, when I started my own small business selling handmade jewelry online, I finally understood what she meant that day.
Narrator: [honestly] Sometimes a customer would ask if a piece was real silver, and part of me wanted to stay vague, because vague answers sold more products.
Narrator: [determined] But I remembered her fabric stall, and I started answering every question completely, even when the honest answer occasionally lost me a sale.
Narrator: [warmly] My business grew slower than some competitors at first, but my customers kept returning, month after month, year after year, exactly like hers once did.
Narrator: [peacefully] She passed away two years ago, but I still hear her voice sometimes, reminding me that trust, once earned honestly, becomes worth more than any single sale.
Narrator: [sincere] I named my business after her last month, quietly, without announcing why, because some tributes feel more honest when they aren't explained to everyone.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's grandmother sell for over thirty years?
quiz.explanation: She sold fabric at the market for over thirty years and was known as Mbah Fabric.

quiz.question: Why did customers keep buying from her even though she wasn't the cheapest?
options: They knew she would never lie about the quality
She was the only seller in town
quiz.explanation: She said customers stayed loyal because they knew she would never lie about the quality.

quiz.question: What did the grandmother do when she noticed a torn piece of fabric?
options: She sold it quickly before the customer noticed
She pointed out the tear even though the customer hadn't noticed it
She hid the torn fabric in the back
She gave it away for free
quiz.explanation: She refused to sell the torn fabric silently and pointed out the tear to the customer herself.

quiz.question: Why did the grandmother consider staying silent about the tear a form of lying?
options: Silence in that moment would have been the same as lying, even without a false statement
She was legally required to speak
quiz.explanation: She believed that silence in that moment would have been the same as lying, even though she said nothing false.

quiz.question: What did the narrator eventually name her own business?
quiz.explanation: She named her business after her grandmother quietly, without announcing why, as a private tribute.
